title: Repeated Windows Installer Installation Failures
exclusions: Detects three or more unique Microsoft Windows Installer (`MsiInstaller`) Application-channel Event ID 11708 records on one Windows host in a closed 30-minute event-time window. It covers Windows Installer/MSI installation failure only. Event 11724 is successful removal and is explicitly excluded; 11707 is successful installation; 1033/1034 status values, patch/update events, repair/reconfiguration, rollback details, package-authored Error-table events, MSIX/AppX, Store, winget, EXE/bootstrapper-only installers, Windows Update, Configuration Manager, Intune, and third-party deployment status need separate semantics. Event 11708 proves that an MSI installation operation failed but does not identify root cause, product criticality, deployment intent, package GUID, user impact, or patch compliance by itself. Product text and rendered Message can be localized or package-authored and are context, not aggregation keys. The strict `failure_count > 2`, 30-minute window, 10-minute close delay, and one-hour throttle are local policy choices rather than Microsoft or Splunk defaults. Missing hosts, missing EventRecordID, duplicate paths, unexpanded messages, or stale Application feeds are source-health issues. This UC does not enable verbose MSI logging, retry or repair packages, change installer policy, delete cache files, restart Windows Installer, or make a compliance attestation.
evidence: After deployment, retain the approved Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows package/version and compatibility record; effective Application-channel input, XML rendering, routing, and index/search RBAC; expected-host/source-health inventory; raw Event 11708 XML with provider, channel, computer, EventRecordID, event time, user/SID where present, insertion values, and rendered message; the `windows_repeated_msi_installation_failures` saved-search definition, ACL, closed-window schedule, dispatch history, result rows, and alert actions; deployment-tool job status and package/change identifiers; any securely handled verbose MSI log produced for the same attempt; dashboard and runbook revisions; threshold approval; bounded exceptions; incident dispositions; and dated positive, negative, provider, duplicate, boundary, late-arrival, localization, field-null, recovery, and upgrade tests. This documentation-only review did not execute an installer, alter logging policy, ingest an event, run SPL, deliver an alert, or create production evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated index with absolute bounds equivalent to `earliest=-40m@m latest=-10m@m`, ingest exactly three XML Application events for `Computer=msi-lab-01.example` at different timestamps inside the same closed 30-minute interval. Each has `source=XmlWinEventLog:Application`, `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`, `EventCode=11708`, provider `MsiInstaller`, and a different nonempty EventRecordID 7001–7003. Set `param1=Contoso Agent` and preserve a rendered failure message. Expect exactly one row with `failure_count=3`, three record IDs, the host, provider, product context, first/last event time, source, and source type.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Expect zero rows for each isolated case: exactly two unique 11708 events; three 11724 successful-removal events; three 11707 successful-install events; EventID 11708 from a provider other than MsiInstaller; three copies of one host/EventRecordID through duplicate collection; three failures split across hosts with neither above two; events only in the newest excluded ten minutes; blank host; blank EventRecordID; wrong Application source or source type; and classic events mixed into the XML contract. Confirm that missing ProductName/param1 does not prevent a correctly identified failure from counting, while its context remains `not_extracted`. A separate source-health control must alert on absent/stale host feeds and direct-plus-WEF duplication. A finite host/deployment exception may suppress notification only after the base row is retained.

dataSources: Windows Application log events generated by provider `MsiInstaller`, collected in XML by Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) to deployment-choice `index=wineventlog`, with exact `source=XmlWinEventLog:Application` and `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`. Required fields are `_time, _indextime, Computer|dest|host, EventCode|EventID, Provider_Name|ProviderName|SourceName, EventRecordID|RecordNumber, Message|RenderedDescription`; `ProductName|param1`, user/SID, level, keywords, and activity ID are optional context and must be verified on the deployed Windows/add-on versions. Event 11708 is the failure authority. Verbose `Msi*.log` files and Configuration Manager/Intune/other deployment job records are incident diagnostics, not silently ingested by this rule.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) for local or Windows Event Forwarding Application-channel XML collection and search-time knowledge. A deployment content app owns `windows_repeated_msi_installation_failures`, source health, dashboards, fixtures, and lookup windows_msi_failure_exceptions.csv. No premium app is required; deployment platforms are optional correlation sources.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog" source="XmlWinEventLog:Application" EventCode=11708 earliest=-40m@m latest=-10m@m
| eval event_id=tonumber(coalesce(EventCode,EventID)), provider=lower(trim(coalesce(Provider_Name,ProviderName,SourceName))), endpoint=lower(trim(coalesce(Computer,dest,host))), event_record_id=trim(tostring(coalesce(EventRecordID,RecordNumber))), product_context=trim(coalesce(ProductName,param1,"not_extracted")), rendered_message=coalesce(Message,RenderedDescription,"not_rendered")
| where event_id=11708 AND provider="msiinstaller" AND len(endpoint)>0 AND len(event_record_id)>0
| stats count AS duplicate_count min(_time) AS event_time max(_indextime) AS last_indextime values(product_context) AS product_context values(rendered_message) AS rendered_messages values(UserID) AS user_sids values(user) AS users values(Level) AS levels values(Keywords) AS keywords values(source) AS observed_sources values(sourcetype) AS observed_sourcetypes by endpoint event_record_id provider
| where duplicate_count=1
| stats count AS failure_count min(event_time) AS first_failure_time max(event_time) AS last_failure_time max(last_indextime) AS last_indextime values(event_record_id) AS event_record_ids values(product_context) AS product_context values(rendered_messages) AS rendered_messages values(user_sids) AS user_sids values(users) AS users values(levels) AS levels values(keywords) AS keywords values(observed_sources) AS observed_sources values(observed_sourcetypes) AS observed_sourcetypes by endpoint provider
| where failure_count>2
| eval threshold_failures=2, aggregation_window_minutes=30, close_delay_minutes=10, use_case="UC-1.2.63"
| table endpoint provider failure_count threshold_failures aggregation_window_minutes close_delay_minutes first_failure_time last_failure_time event_record_ids product_context rendered_messages user_sids users levels keywords observed_sources observed_sourcetypes last_indextime use_case
| sort 0 -failure_count endpoint
description: Reports a Windows endpoint when more than two unique `MsiInstaller` Event ID 11708 installation-failure records occur during one closed 30-minute search interval. The aggregation grain is endpoint; each row retains the record IDs, first/last failure time, optional product/message context, users, and source metadata, while exact duplicate collection paths are rejected.
value: Repeated MSI failures can leave required agents, business software, or approved changes unavailable and can consume a maintenance window through retries and rollback. A provider-verified host signal gives endpoint and deployment teams a bounded set of native records to correlate with the actual package job and verbose installer log without misclassifying successful removals or claiming patch compliance.
implementation: Collect every in-scope host’s Application channel as XML with a supported Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows deployment. Verify provider, Event ID, host, and EventRecordID against Event Viewer before alerting. Save the SPL as `windows_repeated_msi_installation_failures`, run every 30 minutes with a measured ten-minute close delay, and trigger when one host has at least three unique 11708 records. Maintain host-feed and duplicate-path health separately; obtain verbose MSI logs or deployment-console records only through the incident workflow.
visualization: Dashboard `Windows — MSI Installation Failures`: source-health row for expected endpoints, stale Application feeds, duplicate EventRecordIDs, and provider/field drift; single values for affected endpoints and failure records; 24-hour/30-day timecharts; bars by endpoint and optional product context; and an incident table matching the SPL output. Drill down to the exact 11708 XML/EventRecordIDs, adjacent package-authored MsiInstaller errors, 11707 successes, 1033 status, Windows Installer service events, deployment-platform job/package/change data, host reboot/disk/permission context, and a restricted verbose MSI log. Label `not_extracted` product context visibly and never turn missing fields or missing sources into success.
schema: Native Windows Application MsiInstaller Event ID 11708 XML; no asserted CIM-equivalent denominator
dataModelAcceleration: The Windows add-on provides broad Application/Change/Endpoint knowledge for Windows events, but its documentation does not guarantee a CIM dataset preserving provider `MsiInstaller`, Event ID 11708, EventRecordID uniqueness, optional insertion strings, and the closed host-level denominator. A generic Change `tstats count` can mix installation, removal, repair, success, and unrelated events. No `cimSpl` is claimed; a dedicated summary is acceptable only after raw-event identity and boundary parity tests.

knownFalsePositives:
The event and count are real. A benign disposition means the failures arose from approved or understood installer activity, not that 11708 means success.

1. **Microsoft Configuration Manager or Intune retry campaign** — A required application can retry after deadline, reboot, content, detection-rule, or dependency trouble and generate several 11708 records. Correlate exact endpoint, application/package ID, assignment, attempt times, return codes, content status, reboot state, and management-console result. Fix the deployment or dependency; suppress duplicate notification only for a finite incident window.

2. **Win32_Product inventory or compliance query** — Microsoft documents that querying `Win32_Product` can initiate consistency checks and repairs, including 11708 under constrained accounts. Identify the WMI caller, scheduled task, inventory product, command/query, account, timing, 1035 reconfiguration burst, and owner. Replace it with a safer inventory method rather than allowing all installer failures.

3. **Approved package development, QA, or rollback test** — Packaging teams may deliberately exercise broken prerequisites, rollback, upgrade, downgrade, repair, or cancellation on a lab endpoint. Match lab asset, package hash/product code, test case, operator, UTC bounds, and expected failure count. Preserve the result as test evidence and use a time-bound host/test exception.

4. **User cancellation or maintenance-window termination** — A help-desk or interactive user can cancel setup, log off, shut down, or reach a deployment timeout. Confirm package/deployment logs, user/session, change window, cancellation code, reboot/shutdown event, and whether required software remains absent. A required deployment still needs follow-up even when cancellation was intentional.

5. **Already-installed, encrypted/substitute target, or SYSTEM-permission condition** — Microsoft lists these among common 1603 causes. Compare product inventory, target path, EFS/substitute drive, ACL under the actual installer identity, verbose log, and package requirement. Do not infer 1603 from 11708 alone; prove the paired status/log before remediation.

6. **Security software, backup, or application-control interference** — Microsoft Defender, EDR, WDAC/AppLocker, antivirus, backup snapshots, or file locks can block package actions. Correlate Defender/EDR detection, Code Integrity/AppLocker events, locked file/process, package signature, policy revision, and approved software catalog. Never disable security controls globally to clear the alert.

7. **Transient content/share/network failure** — Configuration Manager distribution point, Intune CDN, DFS/SMB share, proxy, DNS, or package source can be temporarily unavailable. Validate deployment download/log status, source path, network errors, cache hash, retry timing, peer impact, and recovery. Keep broad multi-host failures visible because they may indicate shared distribution outage.

8. **Direct plus Windows Event Forwarding duplication** — The same host/EventRecordID can arrive via two collection paths. The primary rule rejects duplicate identities; source health must compare Computer, EventRecordID, source route, subscription, and forwarder. Correct dual authority rather than raising the threshold or arbitrarily deduplicating one path.

**Safe suppression:** use lookup windows_msi_failure_exceptions.csv after the result. Key on exact `endpoint,deployment_id` with numeric inclusive `valid_from_epoch`, exclusive `valid_until_epoch`, owner, approver, ticket, package, and reason. Reject wildcards, endpoint groups, indefinite windows, and exceptions for missing/stale feeds, duplicate routes, unknown provider, or required-security-agent failures. Keep the base finding and raw records. Close only after deployment intent is satisfied or an accepted newer attempt succeeds; silence is not recovery.
mitreAttack: N/A (operational Windows Installer failure monitoring; malicious MSI execution requires separate process/security analytics)
hardware: Windows endpoints and servers that use Windows Installer/MSI packages and expose the local Application event channel. Non-Windows systems, MSIX/AppX-only environments, installers that never invoke Windows Installer, offline images, and management-platform records without corresponding endpoint Application telemetry are outside this event contract.

cost.search_load_notes: The search scans a closed 30-minute slice with index, source type, source, and one Event ID predicates, then performs one event-identity deduplication gate and host aggregation. Application-channel ingest cost depends on total channel volume, not 11708 alone; measure fleet event rate and WEF delay.

detailedImplementation:
## Define the MSI failure boundary

Assign Windows endpoint, software packaging, deployment-platform, Splunk collection/content, source-health, service-desk, and incident owners. Inventory all managed Windows hosts and whether Application events arrive directly, through WEF/WEC, or by one approved alternate route. Select a supported Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows release and qualify it with exact Windows, Universal Forwarder, collector, search-tier, and Splunk platform versions. The collection identity needs Application-log read and forward rights. Search users need the local `wineventlog` index. Neither requires package installation, registry-write, service-control, administrator, Intune, or Configuration Manager mutation rights.

Microsoft's Windows Installer event table is the semantic authority. Error 1708 is “Installation operation failed,” and general installer events add 10,000, producing Event ID 11708. Error 1707 becomes successful installation 11707. Error 1724 becomes 11724 and means removal completed successfully; it must never be counted as an install failure. Other MsiInstaller entries can be useful but carry their own operation/status semantics. Keep this rule narrow rather than treating every MsiInstaller Error-level event as equivalent.

Event 11708 is a terminal operation fact, not a complete diagnosis. Product packages can write other Error-table events; a nearby 1033 status can carry a return status such as 1603; verbose MSI logs contain actions and rollback. Do not label every 11708 “1603,” “patch failed,” “corrupt cache,” or “pending reboot.” Do not claim deployment noncompliance without a desired-state assignment and evaluated deadline from the authoritative management platform.

The policy reports `failure_count > 2` unique records per endpoint in one closed 30-minute interval. Three is the first alerting value. The host—not product text—is the denominator because rendered/insertion fields vary by package, language, event rendering, and add-on extraction. This catches repeated retries while keeping one failure visible on dashboards. Tune window and threshold only after replaying normal deployments and proving boundary behavior.

## Collect the native Application channel as XML

Deploy one governed Application-channel input through the add-on. A local deployment-app stanza may be:

```ini
[WinEventLog://Application]
disabled = 0
renderXml = true
index = wineventlog
checkpointInterval = 5
```

`wineventlog` is a local choice. Add-on 6.0.0 and later defaults Windows events to XML, but keep the intent explicit and test upgrades. XML produces `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog` and `source=XmlWinEventLog:Application` under the reviewed contract. If `$XmlRegex` allow/deny filters are used, prove that MsiInstaller 11708 cannot be dropped. Prefer collecting the complete operationally justified channel and filtering at search time unless license/privacy policy says otherwise.

On WEF/WEC, preserve original `Computer`, EventRecordID, provider, event time, channel, and subscription route. Measure forwarding delay and backlog. Do not collect the same endpoint both directly and through WEC without an intentional transition plan. Restrict Application data because package names, paths, users, command context, and vendor details can be sensitive.

Validate indexed records:

```spl
index=wineventlog sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog" source="XmlWinEventLog:Application" EventCode=11708 earliest=-24h
| table _time _indextime Computer Provider_Name ProviderName SourceName EventCode EventID EventRecordID RecordNumber ProductName param1 UserID user Level Message
| sort 0 Computer _time
```

Compare at least two fixed EventRecordIDs with **Event Viewer > Windows Logs > Application**, provider **MsiInstaller**. Confirm exact Computer, provider, ID, level, time, insertion values, user/SID, and message. Inspect raw XML, not only rendered text. On every supported language/package sample, record which optional field contains product context. The primary rule works when that field is absent.

## Maintain source and duplicate-route health

Track expected hosts with enable/retire epochs, route, collector, owner, and maximum silence. Report missing/stale Application channel, provider/event extraction drift, missing Computer, missing EventRecordID, future event time, excessive `_indextime-_time`, WEF backlog, channel full/cleared, checkpoint reset, duplicate `(Computer,EventRecordID)`, two routes, and unsupported classic/XML mixing.

The search's first `stats` groups exact endpoint and record ID. `duplicate_count=1` rejects a record observed more than once instead of inflating retries. Duplicate events must still appear in source health; do not silently choose one because route disagreement undermines evidence. EventRecordID can restart after a log clear/rotation, so raw channel identity, host, time, and route remain important for long retention. Inside the bounded 30-minute interval, requiring the exact ID is an appropriate uniqueness gate.

No records does not prove installations succeeded. Quiet hosts can be normal, so combine event freshness with forwarder/WEF heartbeat and periodic canary collection. Preserve source-health results separately from installation findings.

## Create and understand the closed-window SPL

Save the sidecar query as `windows_repeated_msi_installation_failures`. Run it every 30 minutes after at least ten minutes of measured close delay. The embedded `earliest=-40m@m latest=-10m@m` selects a 30-minute event-time slice and excludes the newest ten minutes; Splunk's latest bound is exclusive. If p99 WEF/index lag exceeds ten minutes, increase delay while preserving nonoverlapping 30-minute slices.

The base predicate fixes index, XML source type, Application source, and 11708. `event_id` converts only the native ID. Provider and endpoint are normalized for comparison. Provider must equal `msiinstaller`; an unrelated vendor reusing 11708 is excluded. Event record and host must be present. Optional product and message context receives a visible sentinel, never a made-up package.

The first aggregation rejects duplicates and retains context. The second counts unique admitted records by endpoint, captures first/last time, and combines IDs, products, messages, user context, level, and source metadata. The strict final `failure_count>2` is the only threshold. No success/removal event is subtracted, because a later success does not erase that three failures occurred; recovery/disposition belongs in incident state and deployment correlation.

Trigger on any row. Throttle repeated notifications by endpoint and active incident for one evaluation period, but index every result. A product-level alert can be added only after a stable, version-tested product code/name extraction or deployment ID exists. Message regex is not a safe fleetwide identity.

## Validate event semantics and SPL behavior

Load fixed XML fixtures into an isolated index. Run the positive three-record control and assert one row with every expected field. Run negatives independently: two 11708; 11707; 11724; provider mismatch; duplicate identity; host split; latest-excluded events; missing identity; wrong source/type; and optional product null. Test events exactly at earliest and latest boundaries, different `_indextime`, upper/lower provider spelling, EventCode versus EventID, EventRecordID string/numeric types, Unicode product/message text, and very long multi-value messages.

Create separate fixtures for 1033 with success status zero and failure status 1603 to demonstrate why those semantics are not inferred from 11708. Test package-authored events such as 11722 alongside 11708 and ensure only 11708 enters the denominator. Validate classic-mode data separately if legacy collection must remain; do not OR it into the production search until fields and duplicate authority are proven.

On a packaging lab endpoint, install a harmless test MSI successfully and compare 11707. Then run a deliberately invalid or dependency-failing test package under an approved harness and compare 11708 plus its verbose log. Avoid damaging production cache, permissions, or services. Record package hash, command, return code, event IDs, EventRecordIDs, deployment record, log path, UTC interval, and cleanup.

Measure Application events/day, 11708 rate, WEF latency, duplicate rate, search runtime, multi-value result size, and dashboard cardinality. Keep `status=draft` until accountable endpoint, packaging, deployment, and Splunk owners accept versions, source coverage, threshold replay, alert delivery, dashboard/RBAC, diagnostic-log handling, exceptions, and runbook.

## Diagnose with verbose Installer and deployment evidence

When Event 11708 lacks root cause, first retrieve the package/deployment platform's own log and return code. If a controlled retry is approved, `msiexec.exe /i "C:\path\package.msi" /L*V "C:\approved\package.log"` creates verbose output. Microsoft also documents policy/registry logging, but warns not to leave it enabled because of performance and disk-space impact. Prefer per-command logging for a bounded reproduction.

Treat verbose logs as sensitive: they can contain paths, account names, properties, URLs, commands, and package data. Store them under restricted incident retention, redact secrets, and never ingest an entire Temp directory by default. Search around the failed action and rollback; “Return value 3” is a useful diagnostic convention but can be localized and is not guaranteed to identify the original cause in every package.

For 1603, Microsoft lists already-installed software, encrypted target folder, substitute drive, and insufficient SYSTEM permissions among known causes. Establish that 1603 actually belongs to this attempt before following that article. Other codes require their corresponding package/vendor documentation. Check disk space, pending reboot, installer service state, package signature/hash, source/cache availability, application-control/antivirus events, locked files, prerequisite versions, and deployment detection rules without assuming any one cause.

## Operationalize response without dangerous automation

Alert title: `Three or more Windows Installer installation failures in 30m: <endpoint>`. Include count, UTC first/last, record IDs, product context with extraction-confidence label, users/SIDs, close delay, source-health route, deployment owner, active change, bounded exception, and dashboard/runbook links.

Responder order:
1. Verify provider/ID/host/record uniqueness and raw XML against Event Viewer.
2. Determine installation intent through Configuration Manager, Intune, software center, package scheduler, user report, change ticket, or process telemetry.
3. Match package/product code, hash, command, assignment, attempt number, return status, and verbose log to the exact interval.
4. Check shared content/distribution, network, proxy, disk, permissions, encryption/substitute path, cache, reboot, security-control, locked-file, prerequisite, and prior-version conditions.
5. Decide whether to correct package content/detection, repair a dependency, reschedule after reboot, restore source access, contact vendor, or accept the rollback.
6. Re-run only through approved deployment workflow; confirm desired application state and a successful authoritative deployment result. Preserve both failure and recovery evidence.

Do not automatically retry MSI, run repair/uninstall, delete `%windir%\Installer`, clear Temp, grant SYSTEM Full Control broadly, disable Defender/WDAC/AppLocker, restart `msiserver`, reboot, or change Group Policy from this alert. These actions can damage package registration, create outage, or weaken security.

Use lookup windows_msi_failure_exceptions.csv only after the base result and under the exact finite contract in `knownFalsePositives`. Review expected hosts, collection routes, field extraction, threshold/delay, exceptions, and dashboard quarterly and after Windows, add-on, WEF, deployment-platform, packaging, or Splunk upgrades.

## Troubleshooting collection and content

- **11708 in Event Viewer but absent in Splunk:** inspect effective Application stanza, XML mode, filters, checkpoint, forwarder queues, WEF subscription, index route, and permissions.
- **Provider null:** inspect raw XML and search-tier add-on knowledge. Do not trust Event ID alone or substitute rendered `Source` text without validation.
- **Product null:** expected for some renderings/packages. Keep counting provider-verified events and use raw insertion/deployment data for context.
- **Message says error 1603 but no field exists:** preserve rendered text and obtain the paired status/log. Do not fleetwide-regex a localized sentence as authoritative status.
- **11724 appears in an old dashboard:** remove it from failure logic; Microsoft defines it as successful removal.
- **Counts double after WEF rollout:** compare endpoint/EventRecordID and collection route, disable old authority after cutover, and backfill a clean baseline.
- **Required software is missing but no alert:** non-MSI or silent/absent telemetry is outside this event rule. Query authoritative desired-versus-installed state separately.
- **One failure never alerts:** by design the repeated-failure page threshold is three. Keep single failures searchable and route critical package assignments through deployment-specific logic.
- **Late WEF events miss the slice:** measure event/index lag, raise close delay, and replay boundary tests; do not overlap windows casually.
- **CIM Change results differ:** expected because generic Change events do not preserve this exact provider/ID/record denominator.
grandmaExplanation: We notice when the Windows tool that installs business software fails several times on the same computer. We keep the exact records so the support team can find the package and reason, while avoiding successful removals and unrelated installers.
